q: On a graph of f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2} + 1, what does the dashed vertical line x = 2 represent?
o: A vertical asymptote where the denominator hits zero and the curve cannot cross
Setting x − 2 = 0 causes division by zero, creating a forbidden boundary.
The slope of the tangent line at the origin
A tangent line touches the curve at a point; x = 2 never touches the curve.
The total accumulated area under the curve
Accumulated area is shown as a shaded region between bounds, not an asymptote.
A local minimum turning point
1/(x − 2) + 1 has no turning point; x = 2 is an excluded domain value.
e: A vertical asymptote marks an input value excluded from the domain (here x = 2) that the graph approaches without ever touching.

q: Which visual part shows the instantaneous rate of change of a curve at one point?
o: The dashed tangent line and its rise/run triangle
The tangent line matches the curve's exact slope at the contact point.
The hatched shaded region below the x-axis
Shading shows accumulated area (integral), not instantaneous slope.
The horizontal asymptote line
Horizontal asymptotes show long-run end behavior as x grows very large.
The grid tick spacing on the y-axis
Grid ticks only set the measurement scale.
e: The tangent line grazes the curve at one point and its rise/run ratio measures the derivative f'(x₀).

q: In the bias-variance curve, what happens when model complexity moves into the Overfitting zone?
o: Training error stays near zero while validation error climbs back up
An over-complex model memorizes training noise and performs poorly on new data.
Both training and validation errors drop to zero together
Validation error rises on unseen data once the model starts fitting random noise.
Training error rises sharply because the model is too simple
High training error from an overly simple model is underfitting, not overfitting.
The validation curve becomes a vertical asymptote
Validation error curves upward smoothly rather than jumping to infinity.
e: Overfitting happens when extra complexity chases training noise instead of the true pattern, hurting validation accuracy.

q: Why does a comparison table include a Differences filter button?
o: To dim rows where all columns share the same value so trade-offs stand out
Dimming identical rows lets you focus immediately on where models actually differ.
To delete columns that have negative numbers
Column filtering highlights one column; Differences dims rows with matching values.
To sort bars from smallest to largest
Bar sorting is unrelated to comparison table row filtering.
To hide all headers on mobile screens
Mobile comparison tables keep sticky headers visible while scrolling.
e: The Differences toggle keeps identical rows quiet and accents rows where the compared options diverge.

q: In the request pipeline diagram and flowchart, what happens immediately when the Cache Hit? decision evaluates to No?
o: The request queries the Database and then stores the result in Cache
A cache miss falls back to the persistent database before returning the response.
The request immediately rejects the user with an Auth Error
Auth checks occur before the cache lookup; a cache miss is normal, not an auth error.
The client skips the API Gateway
All requests enter through the API Gateway first.
The response is discarded without reaching the client
The database supplies the missing data so the client still receives a response.
e: Cache misses route to the database (slower path), whereas cache hits return straight from fast memory.

q: In a semantic flowchart, why does a decision node use a diamond indicator and amber role color?
o: To show a branching condition that routes execution down different paths
Amber + diamond consistently marks parameter tests and branch conditions.
To show a terminal error state that aborts the system
Terminal error states use the rose error badge, not amber decision.
To indicate raw user input arriving from outside
Inputs use the blue variable/input role.
To mark a final verified output
Final outputs use the green result role.
e: Distinct shapes and colors separate inputs (blue), processes (violet), decisions (amber), outputs (green), and errors (rose).

q: What distinguishes a cycle diagram from a linear flow?
o: The final stage feeds back into the first stage to repeat iteratively
Training epochs, feedback controllers, and biological cycles loop continuously.
A cycle can only have two nodes
Cycles commonly have 3 to 6 stages arranged around a central goal.
A cycle never uses arrows between stages
Directed arcs show the exact clockwise order around the loop.
A cycle cannot be stepped through one stage at a time
Every Kit.cycle visual supports step-by-step playback and clickable stages.
e: Cycles model closed loops where outputs from one pass become inputs to the next iteration.

q: What does a time-scaled timeline reveal that an evenly spaced timeline hides?
o: How long the real gaps were between breakthroughs
Proportional spacing shows clusters of rapid progress versus quiet decades.
Which branch of a tree gets pruned
Branch pruning belongs to search trees, not chronological timelines.
The exact derivative at each year
Timelines order discrete events rather than plotting continuous derivatives.
The database latency of an API request
Latency belongs to system architecture and bar metrics.
e: Setting scale: "time" spaces events proportionally to their numeric dates so clusters and gaps are visible.

q: Why does ID3 place Outlook at the root of the Play Tennis decision tree?
o: It produces the highest Information Gain (0.25 bits), reducing entropy the most
ID3 greedily picks whichever attribute splits the data cleanest at the root.
It has the fewest alphabetical letters
Attribute names have no effect on entropy calculations.
It guarantees 0% accuracy on Overcast days
Overcast gives 100% pure Play = Yes (0 entropy), not 0% accuracy.
It avoids creating any leaf nodes
Pure subsets like Overcast immediately become leaf nodes.
e: ID3 compares Information Gain across candidate features and chooses the largest entropy drop for the root split.

q: When every training example down a tree branch belongs to the same class (entropy = 0), what does the node become?
o: A green leaf node outputting that class
Zero entropy means no further splits are needed—the branch terminates in a leaf.
Another root node that restarts the dataset
Each tree has only one root at the top.
A pruned rose node that must be deleted
Pure leaves are kept as final answers, not pruned.
A vertical asymptote
Asymptotes are graph boundaries, not tree nodes.
e: Zero entropy means pure agreement, so the tree stops splitting and emits a final leaf prediction.

q: In a Minimax tree with Alpha-Beta pruning, why can a MIN node stop checking remaining children once its score drops to or below \alpha?
o: The parent MAX player already has a better option \alpha and will never choose this branch
Because MAX takes the maximum, a MIN branch that can already force <= alpha is irrelevant.
The MIN node wants to maximize its score above beta
MIN minimizes the score; MAX maximizes.
Alpha-Beta pruning randomly drops half the leaves to guess faster
Alpha-Beta pruning is exact—it never changes the optimal Minimax value.
The root node only allows one child
Root nodes can have many moves; pruning only skips provably suboptimal subtrees.
e: Alpha-Beta pruning skips branches that cannot influence the parent's choice, giving the exact same answer faster.

q: Comparing BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, A*, and Alpha-Beta, which algorithm uses a heuristic h(n) to stay both optimal and focused?
o: A* Search (with an admissible heuristic)
A* combines path cost g(n) with admissible heuristic h(n) to prune pointless detours.
Breadth-First Search (BFS)
BFS expands uniformly layer by layer without a heuristic or edge weights.
Depth-First Search (DFS)
DFS dives down one path without checking path cost optimality.
Alpha-Beta Pruning
Alpha-Beta solves two-player adversarial game trees, not weighted shortest paths.
e: A* guides shortest-path search toward the goal using f(n) = g(n) + h(n) while guaranteeing optimality when h is admissible.
